sections.overview: The Canada lynx is a wild cat of northern North America, living in boreal forests from Alaska across Canada and into the northern United States. Its life is closely tied to the snowshoe hare, whose abundance shapes where lynx thrive and how their numbers change.
sections.identification: This medium-sized cat has long legs, broad furred paws, cheek ruffs and narrow black ear tufts. Its short tail ends in black. The coat is usually grayish or buff, sometimes faintly spotted; seasonal fur changes make it look less sleek in summer. Adults average about 80–85 cm in body length. Reported masses are about 4.5–10.0 kg for females and 7.3–17.2 kg for males; males are generally heavier, with ranges that overlap.
sections.habitat: Lynx use a mosaic of forest stands. Dense young growth shelters hares, while older trees, fallen trunks and root mounds provide cover and denning places. In mountain regions, deep winter snow helps define suitable habitat and gives lynx an advantage over some competing predators.
sections.diet: The snowshoe hare is its principal prey, especially in winter. Lynx also take mice, voles, squirrels, grouse and other birds. Alternative foods matter more when hares are scarce or in some southern populations; hungry lynx may roam farther, though substitutes may not nourish them adequately.
sections.behavior: Usually solitary, the lynx moves quietly through cover and hunts mainly by sight and hearing, stalking or waiting by prey trails before an ambush. It may be active day or night, often around dawn and dusk. Scent marks and calls help individuals communicate across ranges.
sections.reproduction: Mating occurs in late winter or early spring. After roughly nine weeks, a female gives birth in a sheltered den among fallen wood. She raises kittens alone. Litter size and breeding success vary with food supply; poor hare years reduce reproduction and kitten survival.
sections.ecology: The lynx–hare relationship forms a predator–prey cycle. When hares are plentiful, lynx find food readily; after hare numbers fall, lynx populations usually decline later. Cycle timing and strength differ by region, so northern patterns do not apply everywhere.
sections.conservation: Risks vary across its range. Habitat fragmentation, trapping, competition with coyotes or bobcats, and changing snow affect local populations, especially near the southern edge. Canada’s 1989 and 2001 national assessments classified it as not at risk; New Brunswick listed it as special concern in 2022.
